speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 159, to amend the Civil Service Act.
He said: It is a recognized fact that bilingualism is the chief factor which ensures understanding and protects true national unity between the two great peoples who share the noble task of developing our country and making it prosperous.
To have a true appreciation of the great cultural and social contribution made to Canada by our English-speaking compatriots, one must understand their mentality, one must be familiar with their literature and one must have exchanged ideas with them. The best way in which French Canadians may achieve these ends is to learn their language.
The same rule applies in the case of our English-speaking compatriots. If they wish to understand us and appreciate the value of our mentality and of our French culture, they
Civil Service Act
must recognize that they too must practise bilingualism. True bilingualism is the straight-est road to understanding, and it cannot be a one-way road.
Bilingualism in Canada is not a conciliatory gesture to ensure understanding; it is not even a question open to discussion. It is our historical vocation; it is a constitutional fact, the principle at the base of confederation. It is not a matter of choice but a constitutional duty to fulfil.
The bill which I am now submitting for the approval of the house does not require that all Canadians be bilingual; it only tends to grant a preference to bilingual applicants in civil service examinations. It would, moreover, fill a need, that bilingual qualifications would henceforth be established by means of examinations. This bill is an invitation to those who enter the Canadian civil service to better adapt themselves to the bicultural character of our Canadian mentality. Such a preference would in no way interfere with the veterans preference now granted by the act but would take second place to it and add a national unity factor to our civil service which is the lifeblood of the nation.
To vote against this bill would be to deny the existence of the two official languages of Canada. To vote against this bill would be to give official approval to the unfortunate slogan: Be bilingual in Quebec and unilingual in the rest of Canada. To vote against this bill would be to strike a hard blow against national unity and force Quebec into isolationism. To vote against this bill would be tantamount to saying to French Canadians that they have made a mistake in learning English and that their group is merely tolerated within confederation.
The growth of true bilingualism among the two main racial groups of Canada has been impeded by the habit of considering these groups on a provincial basis and of wrongly repeating that there are nine English provinces and one French province. This has all too often prevented many of our English speaking compatriots who are well disposed from admitting the necessity of learning French. Such an idea is contradicted by the facts. French-speaking Canadians are distributed in all provinces and in the country as a whole in almost equal number to English speaking Canadians.
According to the most recent government statistics, racial groups in Canada are distributed thus: Canadians of English origin, 47-9 per cent, Canadians of French origin, 30-8 per cent, and Canadians of various other races having emigrated to Canada account for the rest. Canadian unity will be a fact when there are no longer French

Civil Service Act
Canadians or English Canadians but Canadians, period. But this can only be attained when the word "Canadian" encompasses the aspirations of each of the two racial groups which form our country. To act otherwise and to relegate bilingualism to Quebec only is to divide the two great races historically united in the foundation of the great Canadian family.
(Translation):
Mr. Speaker, if it be granted that bilingualism is the main instrument of good understanding and if, on the other hand, we look into the government's attitude and behaviour towards the two racial groups which make up our country, and more particularly into the attention it has given to those who have made an effort to achieve bilingualism, we are faced with a genuine national scandal.
In a speech I made on this matter last year, using figures taken from the public accounts, I compiled a comparative table showing how the two racial groups have shared in the appointments to the higher positions in the federal civil service, namely those over $5,000 per year. I shall not repeat those figures, but I would like to repeat the final result. French Canadians who are bilingual in a proportion of 77 per cent hold but 13 per cent of the higher positions. Even if they had never made their generous effort to become bilingual, in proportion to their numbers, they should have been entitled to at least 30 per cent of the higher positions. Although I sincerely wish to avoid using harsh words, faced with such figures I feel compelled to say that we have been shamefully victimized and that, unless a drastic change comes to pass, we shall have to check this one-way trend towards bilingualism, which can only lead to assimilation.
On one occasion during the last session, before the orders of the day I asked the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Pickersgill), who was then secretary of state, to give figures showing the racial representation of the Canadians in the civil service, according to whether or not they were bilingual. The hon. minister replied that it was not possible for the civil service commission to determine whether an employee was bilingual or not. I was astounded by this reply. In a bilingual country, so proficient in the matter of statistics, it was not possible to determine who was bilingual and who was not! I took the matter up again this year and put to the new Secretary of State (Mr. Pinard) the following question, which appears on page 1881 of Hansard:

1.	Has the civil service commission ever asked for a report on the bilingualism of civil servants of the various departments of the government?
2.	If so, on what date?
3.	What departments have answered?
4.	What is the result of this inquiry?
The hon. minister replied that an inquiry had been made, that certain departments had been unable to give complete answers but that he had obtained them at a later date. As for his reply on the result of the inquiry here it is:
A number of departments indicated that information of a reasonably accurate nature was not available; others based their reports upon unverified claims as to language qualifications. It should be pointed out that it is not easy to know whether or not an employee is bilingual. In a number of cases, it is impossible to answer such a question by an unqualified "yes" or "no" because it is a matter of degree requiring a qualitative evaluation. In the light of the information obtained, the commission concluded that it would not be possible to arrive at any reasonably accurate figure as to the proportion of bilingual civil servants.
But, Mr. Speaker, if it was impossible to arrive at exact figures, we would surely have liked to obtain at least the figures which had been given to the hon. minister.
The hon. minister assures me that he has requested that such an inquiry be made, but we are still waiting for the figures. If the delay is due to the fact that the Frenchspeaking ministers have been too generous towards their own compatriots, I understand why the hon. Secretary of State hesitates to supply the figures. However, on the basis of the minister's statement, one thing stands out clearly, and it is this:	the civil service
commission has no accurate way of determining what civil servants are bilingual.
Mr. Speaker, the bill now before the house would correct that serious anomaly, since it will permit, in the future, to determine who is bilingual. In fact, subparagraph (c) of the bill states that those who will be entitled to benefit from the privilege provided in the bill are:
. . . those who have qualified, by examination, in the knowledge and use of the two official languages of Canada, being the English and the French languages.
Has the minister considered that his reply to my question is not only a serious admission, but confirmation of the fact that the French-Canadians are victims of gross discrimination. In fact, the civil service commission which, by two ministers' own admission, does not know who is bilingual has nonetheless prescribed bilingualism as a prerequisite to employment in the province of Quebec, except in a few rare instances.

I shall mention only the case of the stenographers and typists who must be bilingual if they are French-speaking, but who receive the same salary as their English-speaking fellow workers who are not bilingual. The bill would recognize the merit of our Englishspeaking fellow citizens who have learned French, and would do away with such discrimination.
I could quote innumerable instances of injustices done our compatriots, who have been told and repeatedly that they should learn English to be promoted.
Hundreds and hundreds of instances show with a pitiable truthfulness that the French language is treated as a poor relation, not only in business but more particularly here in the government, which was set up by the constitution as the guardian of the indefeasible rights of the two racial groups.
Even in this house, the French language is looked upon as a poor relation, for even though according to the letter of the law it enjoys the same privilege as the other language, in practice it is but rarely spoken and those who use it are sure not to be understood by the majority of the representatives of our bilingual country.
Those who are primarily responsible for that anomaly, although I do not wish to accuse anyone, are the French-speaking Canadians themselves, because they seldom speak French in the house during the debates.
An English-speaking colleague recently told me that he took exception to Frenchspeaking members always speaking English, thus depriving the English-speaking members of the opportunity of learning our language.
I particularly blame the French-speaking ministers who, except for the Speaker, speak French only when they reply to a question from a Quebec member, but never do so in their official statements. They will perhaps reply to that serious accusation that they do so because it is the only way to be understood.
Every time our French-speaking ministers use that good excuse for not speaking their own tongue, our English-speaking colleagues will surely contend that they do not need to learn our language.
In all governmental agencies, and more particularily the Canadian National, with the possible exception perhaps of the St. Lawrence seaway authority as far as its cheques are concerned, the French language is treated as a poor relation.
My hon. colleague, the member for Beauce (Mr. Poulin), embodied in a bill the magnificent principle he has upheld for years in order to obtain bilingual cheques. We have here another proof that French is treated as

Civil Service Act
a poor relation in a manner which cannot be explained. We have come to the point where we must submit bills to have our most elementary rights respected. And this happens in a country which boasts of promoting unity, peace and concord among foreign nations.
Every time the French-speaking people ask that some of their prerogatives be respected, they are told, as was done for the flag and other similar matters, that they should proceed step by step, that we must not wound the feelings of others, that something has been gained here or there and so forth. By acting thus we again admit that the French people are really treated as poor relations, that their rights have never been truly recognized throughout the nation, but are granted small parcels of those rights with a measuring cup, by the side door, and as a result of persistent struggles.
If the confederation pact had intended to give to the French language the status of a poor relation, the fathers of confederation would never have agreed to it; besides, if that were the case, the constitution would have been drafted otherwise. There is one section only of the British North America Act which mentions languages, and it is section 133, which reads as follows:
Either the English or the French language may be used by any person in the debates of the Houses of Parliament of Canada and of the Houses of the Legislature of Quebec; and both those languages shall be used in the respective records and journals of those houses.
A list is then given of the official records which must be bilingual.
Therefore, both languages are on equal footing. If the intention had been to rank the French language below the English language, instead of saying "Either the English or the French language may be used", it would have been stated that "French may be used". On the contrary, the text is clear: "Either the English or the French language ....".
The remainder of that section deals with compulsory bilingualism in official documents. Commenting on a speech I made last year on bilingualism, the Star Weekly, in its edition of February 19, 1955, contended that there is nothing in the constitution to indicate that both languages are on an equal footing. According to the writer, one of the two languages enjoys a privileged status. Under what section of the constitution? I should like to know, since the only reference to languages which may be employed applies equally to French and English.

Civil Service Act
I know, Mr. Speaker, that a real and commendable movement is under way and gaining momentum among our English-speaking fellow citizens in favour of exchanges between the two racial groups; this necessary effort is more commendable than that of the government, since it is not made compulsory by the constitution.
In the name of national unity, which they must bring about by deeds and not by words, the government is bound to approve this bill and thus show their good faith. They have no reason to reject it since, by this bill, the preference already given to veterans is widened and the inalienable rights of five million Canadian citizens are confirmed. So far, it must be confessed, we have been treated as a conquered race, but if one goes back to the establishment of our government it must be admitted that two-way bilingualism has become the indispensable confirmation of an honourable compromise between two great ethnical forces which, until then, had been facing each other.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO GIVE PREFERENCE TO BILINGUAL CANDIDATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with a great deal of interest to the remarks made first in English and then in French by the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Girard) in connection with the bill he has introduced in the house today.
In the course of his remarks, he referred to an answer given to him by my colleague, the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration and by myself this year about the number of bilingual employees in the civil service. While dealing with this subject, he charged me and my colleague and, in fact, the government we are representing in these matters, with failure to give an adequate reply to his question. In his view, we failed to give an adequate answer because we had found it impossible to supply the figures requested in his question. Yet, in the answer we did give, we pointed out why it had proved impossible for the civil service commission, to whom I had referred the question, to give a complete answer to the question. It is because the civil service commission, this being a matter of degree and requiring a detailed analysis, is unable to tell whether an employee does or does not speak both languages. I felt that the hon. member would not be satisfied with information dealing merely with civil service positions requiring a knowledge of both languages. I am confident he will agree that very many people in this country speak both languages. He will also admit that there are a great many civil servants who, while they speak rather

fluently both languages, did not have to qualify as bilingual when they entered the civil service. Therefore, an answer dealing only with those employees who had to qualify as bilingual would have been inadequate.
He then pointed out that the Frenchspeaking ministers in particular did not avail themselves often enough of the opportunities they may have to speak French in this house. Yet he himself behaved no differently, finding it convenient and useful, if not indispensable, to speak English at the beginning of his remarks. He thus answered his own question.
In fact, I do believe that, in spite of the good will shown by the hon. members generally, there are many whose knowledge of a second language is not sufficient to allow them to understand the remarks made by members of the government; when, for instance, an English-speaking member who does not speak French and understands it but imperfectly puts a question to a member of the cabinet, I do not believe it is logical to answer him in a language which is not his own, which is not his mother tongue.
Mr. Speaker, I think I should add-and I feel sure I am expressing a wish which is shared by the hon. member-that, as long as the majority in this house do not speak both languages and understand them adequately, it will be quite difficult-the hon. member will agree with me if he is sincere, and I believe he is-it will be extremely difficult to suggest to the members of the government that they should answer in French in such circumstances.
(Text) ;
Mr. Speaker, both as the minister responsible to parliament for the civil service commission and as a French-speaking Canadian representing a constituency mostly composed of Canadians of French extraction, I feel it is my duty to express this government's opinion as well as my own views on this proposed legislation which would have the effect, if enacted, of bringing about a very substantial change in our Civil Service Act.
I wish, first of all, to commend the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Girard) for his remarks. After hearing them I feel that he has done his job in all sincerity and that his intentions are to see to it that the principle of bilingualism, which I share with him, be applied as generally as possible in the federal

administration. Although the immediate objective sought through this measure is to grant preference to bilingual competitors in civil service examinations, this legislation presents at the same time another very important feature. The provisions of the amendment tend to reaffirm the principle of bilingualism and have it recognized in the federal administration everywhere in Canada. Even if I intend to oppose the measure for reasons which I will explain later in my remarks, I wish to emphasize immediately that I am in full agreement with the principle of bilingualism this measure contains. In other words, the principle as laid down is undoubtedly sound, but the method of its implementation as suggested in this bill, at least in my opinion, is wrong.
The proposition which I have just stated is twofold and I intend to deal with each part separately. In the first place, I have just affirmed my belief in complete bilingualism and in the use of the two official languages of Canada which I believe must be recognized as the normal method to be used in our relations together. It must be accepted as an historical and constitutional reality, and it is also essential to our peaceful and orderly growth as a nation.
Without claiming to be an expert on constitutional matters or on the interpretation of our laws, customs and practices as they now exist, I should like the house to bear with me for a few moments while I try to analyse, as objectively as possible, our position and status as a bilingual country.
Although there are a number of countries where more than one language is officially spoken, it is difficult to determine in each case the extent to which actual constitutional or legal dispositions have given recognition to the use of different languages. In more than one country a spirit of understanding and a growing practice have gone further than precise legal and constitutional definition in establishing the rules of application of this principle. In Switzerland, for instance, where a multiplicity of languages prevails, the constitution itself recognizes four languages as national languages and three as official. But the constitution does not go further than that and leaves it to practice itself to lay down the rules of application of this government policy of equality of languages. As a Swiss jurist recently wrote about the problem of languages in this great united country:
This small neutral country has proved that, given good will, understanding, welfare and loyalty are not only possible among people speaking different languages, but that those languages themselves mean an enrichment of life.
Civil Service Act
In another country, Belgium, two languages are recognized. But again in so far as languages are concerned in that country, the constitution is very brief and simple. Section 23 of the Belgian code reads as follows:
Use of the languages current in Belgium is optional: it can be regulated only by law, and only for public documents and judicial matters.
That is all the constitution of Belgium says on that matter. In that country also experience has demonstrated that this great people, although speaking two different languages, has always been inspired in peace as well as in war by only one purpose, that of upholding its fine, generous traditions of courage, industry and determination.
I think in Canada the situation is the same. I think that the mere mention of section 133 of the constitution is not enough to determine whether or not this country of ours is* a bilingual country. Here also the nature of our constitutional pronouncements, which have been more numerous because of more frequent changes in the constitution itself, is not sufficient to determine the degree of bilingualism which Canadians have accepted and recognized. Here also there has been, and there is, besides such legal and constitutional dispositions, the unwritten law based on usage and practice which has served us in the implementation of that principal of bilingualism which today has become more than ever one of the important governing factors in our development and progress as a nation.
As I have indicated before, the constitutional position in Canada has often been modified with respect to languages; indeed, the constitution itself had to be modified with changing conditions. The situation has changed with the constant demographic, political and economic variations which this country has known in her yet short but dynamic history. In a little more than two centuries Canada, from the status of a French colony and later that of a British possession, has grown gradually and step by step to the full stature of a free and sovereign nation and member of the commonwealth. With these gradual changes in its political status, our country has also experienced, as a result of its great development, very serious changes in both the demographic and economic fields. Our system of government, in order to adapt itself to such important variations and trends, has seen its constitution modified often to meet the challenge of such ever changing conditions.
It is interesting to follow the effect of each of these political changes on the progressive recognition of the principle of bilingualism as it is being accepted now in Canada. At the beginning, under the royal proclamation

Civil Service Act
in 1763 which had to serve as the new colony's constitution, no reference was made to the use of the two languages, French and English, by the new government of Quebec which was created by the crown. Three other similar governments were created under the same proclamation for these other new British possessions covering a vast territory in all of North America which France had ceded to Great Britain. This was, of course, as indicated in the proclamation itself, a temporary arrangement to be applied only until a local system of government could be properly organized and functioning in each of these new British possessions.
Under the Quebec Act, religious privileges and others were officially recognized but no direct reference was made yet to the use of the French language in the administration of th* country. Of course, it is not necessary for me to say that obviously ever since 1759 the French language continued to be used in practice and also both in the legislative council and the assembly. But later in 1791, at a time when there was still a large majority of Canadians of French origin, Canada obtained from the new mother country her first real constitution, which was in fact the original authority to organize a responsible government.
The principle of bilingualism is to be found in the terms of that first constitution under which both the people and those whom they chose to elect as their representatives in the legislative council and assembly were given the privilege of taking the oath in the English or French languages as the case required. In 1840, when it was considered advisable to unite into one the two provinces of upper and lower Canada, this privilege of bilingualism was denied. It was then enacted that the English language alone was to be used. This is not the occasion to comment on the wisdom of the change made at that time but it will be recalled that Louis Hippolyte Lafontaine, in a declaration full of dignity and pride, at that time expressed his disagreement with the new provision of the union act.
Our country, which had already known and lived through difficult times, was again put to the test and again tolerance and understanding were to prevail over hatred and prejudice. If such a process may appear at times to be much slower, it does achieve much more efficient and durable results.
Finally, in 1867, when confederation was established as the system of government which was to endure and become the charter of our rights, the principle of bilingualism was again reaffirmed by the four provinces which decided to unite themselves into that dominion to be known as Canada.

As the hon. member indicated, section 133 defines in very clear terms the nature of such bilingualism by proclaiming the French and English languages as the official languages of the parliament of Canada.
Although the section is quite clear, the provision could lend itself to different interpretations which would have the effect of either restricting or extending its terms. But again I say that, in Canada, bilingualism is a matter where legislation alone is not sufficient to determine what the legislature at that time had in mind and what in the country is the position of bilingualism.
Many other factors have to be analysed if one wishes clearly to ascertain whether Canada can rightly claim to be a bilingual country. This again is a matter of degree, as is bilingualism itself. There is bilingualism in theory, of course, as there is bilingualism in practice. If by bilingualism we mean that everyone in Canada must speak both languages, then, of course, Canada, no more than Belgium or Switzerland, is a bilingual or a multi-language country. But if the two languages may be spoken in every province, although the practice may not have been considered necessary in all the legislatures, if the two languages are generally used by a great number of people in all spheres of activity, if it is the overwhelming wish of all Canadians to consider the other language as their second language, these facts must of course be taken as convincing evidence of bilingualism as it exists today in Canada.
I could add a number of other instances which would substantiate such a contention. Let me read, for instance, a few remarks made by the Prime Minister in 1943 when he was then the Minister of Justice and was dealing in the house with a proposed amendment to our constitution:
Section 133 of the constitutional act deals with the matter of languages. It provides for bilingualism in this house, in this parliament, in its journals, in its records and acts, and in the pleadings and processes of the courts of Canada established under the act, to the same extent and just as fully as it provides for bilingualism in the proceedings of the Quebec legislature and the Quebec courts.
I am satisfied that the day will come when, if not all those who sit in this house, at least its leaders and those who grace the treasury benches and those who sit immediately opposite, will find it to their advantage to be bilingual. I do not suggest that we from the province of Quebec are going to try to impose our language upon anybody, but I do suggest that the time will come when those whom I have indicated will find it to their advantage to learn and to understand and to use the French language as we from Quebec have found it to our advantage to learn and to understand and to use the language in which I am speaking at this moment.

These were remarks made by the Prime Minister at the time and I think that I expressed those sentiments when a few moments ago I said that it is not always possible and I should think advisable to answer questions that are being put to the ministers by the members of this house in one language that will not be the language that the hon. member putting the question will understand; and it is to be hoped, as I said earlier, that the day will come when the majority at least of the members of this house will be able to speak fluently both languages, the result being that at that time it will be possible for each minister to answer in either of the two languages.
If the principle of bilingualism has been recognized, as I said, in our British North America Act, if it has also been recognized by custom and practice, if it has been recognized by a greater number of people using both languages in business as well as in other kinds of transactions, I say that it has also received the support of constant action by the government and also by definite corroborative legislation.
The terms of section 133 of the British North America Act have been extended to a great number of administrative measures by the successive governments: two of the most striking examples have been the adoption of bilingual postage stamps and paper currency. When these two decisions were taken by parliament they were not to be termed as concessions by the English-speaking majority to the French-speaking element of our country. It was simply the result of good faith on the part of all the different ethnic groups in Canada, and of parliament's understanding and harmony between the races of the country; it was simply, in effect, the recognition of bilingualism as an essential right of the Canadian citizen.
This right of bilingualism was recognized in that way by parliament in the two precedents to which 1 have just referred; that is, in the use of postage stamps as well as in paper currency, but it was also strongly supported, I believe, by a growing practice both in the House of Commons and outside of a greater number of people accepting the use of the two languages on an increasing number of occasions.
This growing tendency, this definite trend, is to me stronger evidence than words of law of the bilingualism of the land at the moment. But if I have decided to oppose this bill I must say that I do so with some regret. If the proposed measure was only another way of reaffirming my belief in this principle of bilingualism, with which I have already expressed my agreement and with which I believe everyone in this house is in agreement
Civil Service Act
also, I would gladly support it, but I think we are concerned with something quite different when we accept the change of policy contemplated by this proposal.
What is involved in the amending legislation is the granting of a preference to bilingual competitors who wish to enter the civil service of Canada. It may not be necessary to underline as a preliminary remark the very great importance of our civil service in the administration of a country such as ours. Under our democratic system it forms part as an essential entity of one of the most important branches of the government. What the legislature chooses to enact for the good functioning of our democracy, the civil servants must put into application. What parliament decides, the civil service must apply, in other words.
It follows as a result that if we are to have a healthy nation, we must have a competent civil service. I think it can safely be said that parliament could not properly discharge its obligations to the people without the benefit of a competent body of civil servants. Democracy could not operate without the assistance of those who are called upon to apply the measures which the elected representatives of the people have decided to adopt.
Canada prides herself, and should be allowed to continue always to do so, on one of the most efficient of civil service organizations. This is more important today than ever with the ever-increasing commitments which our country must face to keep its place in the forefront. But I believe that what we are concerned with today is something different from what the principle of bilingualism implies. What we are concerned with is to decide whether or not competence should give place to bilingual qualifications in the civil service. I am in favour of as many bilingual civil servants as possible, and I believe I may have the right to say that I have had some humble share in that respect, but I cannot accept that bilingualism should take the place of competence in the choice to be made of our civil servants anywhere in Canada.
Under the act as it now stands, preference is given to war veterans, and the hon. member has made an allusion to that preference which is given to war veterans. The principle in that case is not to be compared, I believe, with that of a preference to be granted to bilinguals.
More than one reason justifies such a policy of preference to apply with regard to those who have served their country in war.
In the first place it is only just and fair to give to those who have been away from the

Civil Service Act
country during a certain period of time and who, in order to accomplish their duties on the battlefields, had to leave their civilian occupations, a treatment similar to that which is afforded to those who have remained in civilian life. The experience of which they have been deprived due to their absence should not, in this case, be a reason for their failure to integrate themselves in the community after their return.
I should say also, and this in my opinion is the real underlying motive for this preference to overseas veterans, that the least a country can do to honour those who have risked their lives to protect and defend it is to assure them of an even chance to re-establish themselves in civil society.
There are no similar considerations, I believe, of national interest involved in the present case which are strong enough to prevail, in my opinion, over the requirement of competence to which I have already referred.
If the provision as advocated under this amending bill was enacted, it would in practice mean that any bilingual candidate although less competent would qualify over other applicants for any position within the civil service.
To illustrate this, it would mean that even where bilingualism will not be needed by a civil servant in the performance of his duties to the public, a bilingual applicant would be preferred to others who would be more competent but would not enjoy the privilege of being bilingual.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO GIVE PREFERENCE TO BILINGUAL CANDIDATES
speechtext: Will the hon. Secretary of State allow me a question?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO GIVE PREFERENCE TO BILINGUAL CANDIDATES
speechtext: Certainly.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO GIVE PREFERENCE TO BILINGUAL CANDIDATES
speechtext: Is the hon. Secretary of State suggesting that when a veteran lacking proper qualifications applies for a job, it is the minister's duty to give it to him?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO GIVE PREFERENCE TO BILINGUAL CANDIDATES
speechtext:
No. I think I have made my position clear enough on that point. The thing that justifies the preference given to veterans before all else is the fact that, since they had to give up their civil occupation and were thus deprived of the experience which otherwise they would have acquired, they have lost all contact with civil life. When the veteran comes back after one or several years, he is in a position where, in order to re-establish himself in civil life, he has lost the experience which otherwise he would have acquired if he had stayed here.

That is what I tried to explain. I believe it is only fair that the government should make up for that period of time when the civil servant went and fought for his country, and during which those who joined the armed forces lose the benefit of the time they were away. I added that one of the reasons which, I think, justify the preference granted veterans, and it may be the main reason, is that they had to go away for a certain time, and it is therefore necessary to make up for their years of absence, so that they can reestablish themselves in civil life and be on an equal footing with others.
It is my belief that this principle does not likewise apply to preference with respect to bilingual people; that is what I attempted to demonstrate.
I believe that, in the civil service, what should count first and foremost, is ability. In my opinion, if, only because he is bilingual, a candidate should obtain preference over someone else who is not, for any position, whether the two languages are needed or not, that would be a danger. I don't think it could be said, for instance-and the problem must be considered in two different lights to a competitor in a constituency where the great majority of the population is Frenchspeaking that whoever speaks both the languages, though he might have got only 70 per cent of the marks in the examination, will obtain preference over a competitor whose sole language is French, even though the latter might have got almost one hundred per cent of the marks. The same kind of reasoning Could be resorted to in the case of a competitor in a constituency overwhelmingly English-speaking.
I think that we would thus agree to and confirm the principle of bilingualism, but we would at the same time very seriously affect the competence of our civil servants. I wonder whether my hon. friend has clearly understood the remarks I just made.
There is no doubt that the fact of bilingualism must be stressed and that the knowledge of both languages is an advantage. Besides, I trust it is admitted and applied by the civil service commission when establishing a competitor's marks. However, I believe, we must not, by adopting the provisions of this bill, recognize the principle that a bilingual candidate would eliminate another who, knowing but one language, would have obtained higher marks at a civil service examination. I think this would be the main danger to which the bill would expose the government and the civil service commission. And that is the main reason why I cannot agree with the proposed legislation, and why I shall vote against it.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO GIVE PREFERENCE TO BILINGUAL CANDIDATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened to the remarks of the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Girard) on bilingualism. I share some of the opinions he expressed, which tend to summon the idea of a heaven on earth, but I must say that the principles he outlined and his bill could hardly be accepted, as the Secretary of State (Mr. Pinard) just pointed out.
If we were to employ bilingual civil servants exclusively, it could happen that a bilingual candidate obtaining only 70 per cent of the marks on some examination would be preferred to a unilingual candidate who might have obtained most of the marks and would deprive the latter of the position he was seeking. My hon. friend should know that such principles are inapplicable to a certain extent. I might point out to him that bilingualism did progress in the past 25 years. Today a greater number of Canadians speak both languages. Greater insistence on bilingualism would be detrimental to many officers and employees of the civil service commission in the province of Quebec.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MEMBERSHIP OF BOARD FROM THREE TO FIVE
speechtext: Is the minister not going to say something about it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MEMBERSHIP OF BOARD FROM THREE TO FIVE
speechtext:
The resolution, I think, explains itself. However, I think I ought to add that the purpose of the resolution, that is, increasing the membership of the tariff board, is brought about by the increased work that the board is doing and has to do under the appeals with respect to both the Excise Tax Act and the Customs Tariff, and also because of the present government
Tariff Board Act
policy of referring more items for consideration to the tariff board so that it might report to us.
We have found that the present membership is not sufficient to discharge these duties as quickly as we would prefer to have them done. As I think there will continue to be an increasing load upon them to deal with the appeals that are being made from the decisions of the deputy minister of customs, and since I think that is the proper thing to happen in our taxing law, I am suggesting to the house that we should increase the membership to five and break down the board, if necessary, into two groups to deal with these things. I am not suggesting that we are dividing the jurisdiction between two parts of the whole but that there may be two committees which could work on different things at the same time.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MEMBERSHIP OF BOARD FROM THREE TO FIVE
speechtext:
I was rather hoping that the minister might go into the matter at somewhat greater length. I might perhaps be allowed to make a personal reference at the outset, to express the regard I have for the present chairman of the board and also to recall that I knew very well the Hon. George Sedgewick, who was, I think, the first chairman and who also was a very highly regarded chairman.
The minister has told us in a general way about the increased work and, in particular, about the number of appeals which come to the board and which, I suppose, are a special aspect of this work. I should like him to give a little further indication as to just how the work will be divided. He spoke about working in more than one group. I wish he would also say something in more detail about the nature of the inquiries that are now being made. Perhaps, if there is nothing confidential about it, he will give us a list of the examinations that are being made.
I should also like to know how they are initiated. Are they initiated by the minister or do they arise from the initiative of the members of various industries? I would like the minister to go into that at some length because, after all, I think the tariff is becoming more and more a matter of importance. We had about 15 blessed years when we seemed to be able to live without tariff questions being projected at us constantly, but it looks now as if perhaps that time was over.
I read with considerable concern in the New York Times of Sunday, April 22, of the large number of appeals for increased tariff assistance that are being made in the United States. Some of them affect us very closely. I read that the wool manufacturers are planning a drive to get the tariff raised. The

Tariff Board Act
same applies to fish products, of which we have heard before, to wood products and others. I mention this because, as I say, these questions are urgent. We know that, in spite of the general over-all prosperity, in spite of the large gross national product, we have areas of distress. I should be glad if the minister would say something at more length than he has on the problem as he sees it and as to the way in which he means to deal with it.
I have in my hands a copy of Foreign Affairs for October 1955, with an article by the principal of Queen's University, Dr. Mackintosh, who worked here as a special member of the finance department for years. I should think that, if there is anyone who by nature is not only in favour of multilateral trade but would look with great aversion on tariffs as a kind of natural enemy, it is he. Nevertheless, I read here in this article statements of concern and of anxiety by him as to the situation, not merely caused by the actual United States tariff but perhaps even more by the customs regulations, which of course we have heard referred to very often here. In particular, he raises the question of the difficulty in which the United States administration finds itself, whereby it is often not able to carry out its contracts. He says, on page 123 of this article:
There are signs that we are entering a period when other countries may press American representatives to produce evidence that the United States is able to make a dependable agreement. To say this is not to discount the ingenious and sincere efforts which have been made by two administrations in Washington to further the aim of larger and more competitive trade in the western world. In future, however, if agreements are to be subject to the heavy discount of escape clauses and modifying legislation, a much greater consideration may be required.
I have made these two references merely to suggest to the minister that these matters are acquiring an importance which probably he and I both deprecate. This party has made perfectly clear its disposition in the matter of trade by the way we have gone along with the various agreements under GATT, but on the other hand we have to face the fact, as Dr. Mackintosh says, that the professions and desires of the United States government are not always backed up by the performance of the officials who administer the law. Having said that, I wish the minister would speak to us and give us a picture of the situation as he sees it, of what the tariff board is doing now and what plans he has, and in general take us a little more into his confidence.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MEMBERSHIP OF BOARD FROM THREE TO FIVE
speechtext:
There are one or two questions I wish to ask, but they are on a different

matter. Perhaps the minister would rather reply to the hon. member for Greenwood at this time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MEMBERSHIP OF BOARD FROM THREE TO FIVE
speechtext:
The tariff board is presently almost fully engaged in the consideration of the tariff items with respect to primary iron and steel. That was a reference which was made to them some months ago, and I must say it is a long and quite cumbersome procedure to cover all the ground that has to be covered, having in mind that the particular tariff schedules had not been dealt with in any general sense since 1907. This in itself would be sufficient work for a board of three at the present time. In addition, however, I was hoping to have the board, as I said we proposed to do in the budget address a year ago, consider the tariff schedules on chemicals, and I think perhaps that has been done recently. If not, it is going to be done at any time now. In the budget address of this year I also referred to the possibility of asking the board to report to us on the radio and television business. It would seem, in my view at least, that there will be considerable work of this kind which will require lengthy and full-time consideration for at least a period of time. But in between all this the tariff board has to deal with appeals from decisions of the deputy minister of customs with respect to various interpretations placed upon the customs tariff and the Excise Act.
While I would not like to use the word "law", because as a matter of fact it is usually fact, nevertheless the results of the decisions of the board in these matters are either accepted by the government as being the interpretation of the appropriate customs tariff item or possibly legislation is brought forward to change it if in the view of the government the decision does not reflect the policy of the government in this particular regard. Many persons who are subject to these imposts are using the appeal system, and I look forward to the work increasing from time to time. Indeed, as I said a moment ago, I think it is the best way in which law can be made. Parliament should do its best to pass law which is understandable and under which traders can conduct their business with confidence, but if there is any doubt in their mind or if in accordance with well established practice they feel they can escape an impost or tax there ought to be a body to which they can go and seek to obtain the interpretation they place upon the particular statute that is causing them difficulty.
For these reasons I am sure that hon. members will agree that at least at the moment, and as long as the government follows the practice of referring questions for report

under the Tariff Board Act, it would seem likely that the board would not be able to keep abreast of its work. I must say that they are doing very well, but at the same time in this particular field no one wants delay in knowing what the law or tax may be. As I personally feel that this work will grow and, indeed, I hope it will grow for the reasons I have given, that we want an established law in this field, I think we ought to increase the number of members in order that no one will be delayed in his ordinary business transactions.
In the very general sense that my hon. friend asked me, may I point out that these inquiries are directed by the minister under section 4 (2), I believe, of the act by virtue of which the minister may ask for information or a report on any given subject. In the course of the period of time that I have been Minister of Finance we have had two reports, one on the textile trade and one on potatoes. I have also indicated the other items that are being considered at the moment.
If the hon. member for Greenwood will forgive me, I would prefer not to say very much about the general world trade and tariff situation because I think he may have seen in the papers there is a report, which the government has not confirmed but which I will confirm now, that certain negotiations have been going on and have been completed at Geneva. I fancy that the results of those negotiations will be made known to the house by my colleague, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, probably in the course of two or three weeks, and it may be that on that occasion or on his estimates or at some other time we might choose to have a debate on GATT and allied subjects. I would be glad to say something then because personally I disapprove of the use of escape clauses except under the most urgent need. But I do not think that our neighbours to the south have perhaps been accurately dealt with when some people say that they have used the escape clauses to a greater extent than they might. I think there is a case to be made for our trade relations with the United States and the results under GATT with respect to that country have been reasonably good over the last six or seven years. I would be glad to make that case if it is not made by someone else.
At the same time I am quite satisfied that the longer we continue the present policy of having frequent meetings, having understandings on frequent occasions and having bindings of our tariff schedules for a period of time-in this case I think it has been two years-the better it will be for everyone
Tariff Board Act
concerned. I am quite satisfied that as time goes by this process will be accepted by the nations of the world and there will be a greater opportunity for a firmer view that trade after all should not have very many restrictions against it. I need not make the qualification that all of us do have tariffs of one kind or another. Presumably every country will always have a tariff of some kind or another, but I do feel that GATT was a great step forward and I do feel that this government is quite proper in its support of it. Indeed, I think all members of the house have supported it at one time or another and in fact, I do not recall that very many exceptions have been stated at any time.
If the hon. member for Greenwood will permit me I will leave the matter that way because I do think there is this other opportunity to discuss it and it would be a better opportunity because under the Tariff Board Act hardly any of the activities of the board have to do with tariff matters in the sense of external relations except those reports I call for. It may be that a tariff board decision would render the admission of an item free of duty whereas the government may have thought that it was subject to an impost. There may also be the opposite case where the government thought that an item was free of duty and a decision was made that it was dutiable. But the number of occasions on which there would be any great variation would not be so great that the activities of the board itself would be a matter which in this manner would affect our trade relations with another country.

speechtext:
If the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre will allow me to ask a supplementary question, I do not imagine there will be much difficulty agreeing with the minister that it is desirable to extend the membership of the board. Indeed, my query is really almost in the opposite direction. I inferred from what the minister said that the inquiry into the chemical industry which he forecast a year ago has not been made. I assume, therefore, that the board has had too much other work and I raise the question whether, in view of the appeals which I gather are increasing in number, the minister is going to be able to have these inquiries completed fast enough for his purposes. That is a matter on which he will have to reach his own conclusion, but it would be a pity if important information was not available to the minister in time. After all, I take it that the making of tariffs depends primarily on knowing your case thoroughly, and I raise the question whether the government is keeping a close watch to

Tariff Board Act
see that this information is coming forward fast enough and, if not, taking steps to that end.
I suppose it is conceivable that they might farm out some of these inquiries as they have done in other cases, but I am making the point merely because I gathered when the minister was speaking that the board has not been able to proceed with the inquiry into the chemical industry and I was struck by that fact. I think it would be a pity if the government found itself in a position where it was not able to act without substantial delay by reason of the necessary research material not being available.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MEMBERSHIP OF BOARD FROM THREE TO FIVE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there are one or two questions I should like to ask. I suppose the answers to some of them are obvious but it is always good to get them on the record. First of all, can the minister tell us what will be the amount of the salaries of the two additional members? I believe there are three different salaries for the three present members of the board, including one salary for the chairman, another for the vice-chairman and another for the third member of the board. What would be the salaries of the two additional members? Also, can he say whether the other conditions that obtain, such as the ten-year tenure of office, the age of retirement and so on, will apply to the two new members?
My other question relates to the statement the minister made that it was his thought that the board would divide into two parts so that two investigations or two inquiries could be under way at the same time. In that connection I should like to ask him whether any change is to be made in subsection 2 of section 5 of the act which already gives two members of the board power to conduct an inquiry under certain subsections of section 4. It does not include subsection 2 which is the subsection under which the minister makes references to the board. In this connection there are one or two points that strike me. It seems perfectly proper that, when you have a board of three, two of them-who after all constitute a majority of the board-should be given the powers of the board. But when you have a board of five is it appropriate that two-who would constitute only a minority of the board- should be given the powers of the board? Will there be some arrangement whereby a decision or a report arrived at by two members of the board will be submitted to a meeting of the full board? It is fairly obvious that it would not seem to be a report of a board of five if that report is made by only two of its members.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MEMBERSHIP OF BOARD FROM THREE TO FIVE
speechtext:
To answer the first question first, may I say that there is no change in the salaries. We shall have three salary levels, namely that of the chairman at $16,500; the vice-chairman at $14,500 and ordinary members at $13,500. However, we shall have two vice-chairmen. At that rate we shall have two paid at $14,500.
With respect to the other question, I suppose one ought to answer

and the time was not so long ago when at this stage on a bill this was the answer made-"wait until you see the bill", but we seem to have grown out of that practice.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MEMBERSHIP OF BOARD FROM THREE TO FIVE
speechtext: I think my question was more germane than were some of the others that have been answered.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE MEMBERSHIP OF BOARD FROM THREE TO FIVE

Resolved, that it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Income Tax Act and to provide, among other things:
1.	That for the 1956 and subsequent taxation years in the taxation of employees who are beneficiaries under an employees profit sharing plan, (a) gains and losses of the trustee under the plan in connection with investment transactions shall not be taken into account in calculating the income of the employee; (b) such part of any amount received by the trustee as a dividend from a taxable corporation as is taken into account in calculating the income of the employee shall be deemed to have been received by the employee as such a dividend for tax credit purposes; and (c) there shall be excluded in calculating the income of an employee

for the period of his first three years as a beneficiary under the plan any amount contingently allocated to him if, within that period, the employee does not become entitled to receive that amount upon his withdrawal from the plan.

3.	That for the 1956 and subsequent taxation years uncertainty regarding the applicability of outstanding regulations respecting depletion allowances be removed.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext: The house again in committee of ways and means on a certain proposed resolution respecting the Income Tax Act. Shall this resolution carry?

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, it is difficult to make a great story about the changes in the Income Tax Act this year. We said we found little in the budget and this is a small fraction of even that budget. With respect to the employee's profit-sharing plan, I wonder whether we might ask for some explanation with regard to the kind of transaction which would be involved in this legislation? In particular will the minister go through (a), (b) and (c) and just expound the situation?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the special provisions with respect' to profit-sharing plans are set out in section 79 of the Income Tax Act. As hon. members know, under this section if a trustee is appointed to receive profits set aside for the benefit of an employee, regardless of whether or not he receives those profit's for probably a considerable number of years, they are considered to be income within the year in which they are allocated. However, representations have been made that even though the employee does not receive the benefit of the income and has to pay a tax on it, which in itself is sometimes objected to but is considered to be a benefit and therefore taxable, there are other factors that do permit income tax concessions that have not been utilized when the income is paid to the trustee of a profit-sharing plan. One, of course, is the matter of capital gain or losses. If there was a capital gain in the hands of an individual, as hon. members know, there is no capital gains tax. With respect to gains or losses on the funds that are handled by the trustee, these will not be taken into account in calculating the taxable income of the employee. What he will pay income tax on will be simply the amount that has been allocated to him in that year by the employer. Then under (b) the complaint that has been received that the trustee is not entitled to take advantage of the dividend tax credit provision is corrected. This would be available for an individual receiver of a dividend from a corporation that has paid Canadian taxes. The
Income Tax Act
trustee will be able to deduct the usual dividend tax credit and the income will not as formerly be fully charged to the employee as taxable income. Then, under clause (c) it has been found that sometimes income has been allocated to an employee, but under the terms of the plan he has no vested interest in this allocation unless he stays in the employment of that particular employer for a certain period of years. I must express amazement that this change has been brought in. The parliamentary assistant says that it is an attempt to restore the administrative practice, but it reminds me of a chapter in income tax history which, I am sure, is still in the memories of a good many who are here in the house.
A number of years ago there was general provision that the membership fees that certain people paid could be deducted for income tax purposes. Apparently it was intended by the government at that time that the deductibility of those membership fees should apply only in the case of persons who were on gross income, the kind of income that doctors and lawyers obtain by receiving fees and paying out certain expenses, in other words selfemployed persons.
However, as hon. members recall, there were, once upon a time, a couple of trade unionists who sought the same deductibility for their trade union dues. They took their case right to the Exchequer Court of Canada, which ruled that, under the law as it formerly read, they were just as much entitled to that deductibility as were doctors and lawyers. The government, shortly after that, following the course of procedure to which the Minister of Finance referred a moment ago, brought in an amendment to the act to change it and make it clear that people on net salaries or wages would not have the privilege of deducting their dues to the organization with which they were connected.
So for a number of years we had the situation under which lawyers and doctors as professional people who received fees and were allowed to deduct expenses, were permitted to deduct their dues to the bar association or the medical society. On the other hand, during that same period, trade unionists on wages and school teachers on salaries were not permitted to deduct their membership dues to their trade unions or their teachers' associations. The same limitation, I may say, was imposed on any doctors or lawyers who were on staffs of various institutions and, consequently, on salaries.
Despite the fact that, to the income tax authorities and to the Minister of Finance at that time, this line of distinction seemed to have some sense, it did not have sense in the eyes of the general public. It certainly did not appeal to the trade unionists of this country, who were denied the right to deduct their trade union dues, whereas most doctors and lawyers were being allowed to deduct their dues to the bar association or the medical society. Consequently, as members will recall, a few years after the period to which

I have in my hand a copy of the judgment contained in tax appeal board cases, volume 10, 1954. It is the case of John Leonard McLeavy v. the Minister of National Revenue, which was heard before W. S. Fisher, Q.C., on February 19, 1954. This document states that:
The appellant, an aircraft maintenance engineer, . . . was required by the terms of his employment to supply his own small tools.
He claimed a deduction under section 11 (10) (c) of the 1948 Income Tax Act. The minister disallowed the deduction on the ground that the appellant's income was from salary and as such could not be reduced by any deductions other than those specified in section 5. The finding makes it clear that the judge was quite sympathetic to the position in which this aircraft maintenance engineer found himself because at one point he does say:
Indeed it would appear that the appellant's claim was a reasonable one in the circumstances.
He goes on to make it clear that the only reason he is disallowing the appeal is that of the existing terms of the Income Tax Act. As he points out in the finding:
The appellant's income is obtained as an employee and his salary, as such, comes within the provisions of section 5 of the 1948 Income Tax Act under which income from an employment may not be reduced by any deductions other than those specifically provided for in the said act. There is no provision in the act, so far as I can discover, under which the appellant, as an employee, could obtain a deduction in respect of depreciation on the small tools owned by him.

The real distinction is the nature of your income, whether it is from self-employment or whether you are on salary or wages.
In that connection, Mr. Chairman, it seems to me that here within the group which it is supposed is getting this deductibility there is an element of discrimination. I am not concerned about the charge the hon. member for York West made against me when I complained that some were not getting this and others were. After all; that is the argument

we are always making when we ask for equity in tax matters. But even within the group of doctors themselves the fact is there are some doctors, those who are self-employed, who are getting this deductibility and there are other doctors on the staffs of our great institutions-as a matter of fact, I have some doctors and some institutions in mind-who gain just as much medically and professionally and for the good of the country by going to these conventions but will not get this deductibility. In my view those hon. members, who tonight have said that this matter has not been thought through sufficiently by those who have presented it to us have been quite correct.

I think anyone who has ever been involved in municipal affairs realizes that very often because it involves the expenditure of public funds municipalities do not pay the expenses of their professional people who attend conventions where the professional person acquires considerable knowledge and from where he brings back to his job the advantage of the knowledge acquired.
That is not the reason I have risen at this time. I would like to ask the minister a question. I was somewhat intrigued by the case put forward by the Minister of National Revenue with respect to who should and who should not be permitted to deduct expenses for attending conventions, and from long years of experience in attending conventions, mostly at my own expense, I do know that there is a vast difference between the representation at those conventions by individuals and the attendance by employees of large corporations.
What I want to ask the Minister of Finance is this. Does the word "taxpayer" mean corporation?
